extracted.intended_audience: researchers, editors, journalists, and general readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and reporting instances of research misconduct, retractions, and integrity-related developments across the scholarly literature and related events. The page aggregates news items that illustrate problems such as fabricated citations, image manipulation, plagiarism, and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated citations / hallucinated references
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that referenced a paper that didn’t exist; an audit found about one in 277 PubMed-indexed papers in early 2026 referenced a non-existent paper, a sharp increase coinciding with the rise of AI writing tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis by Topaz et al. used AI to distinguish genuine fabrications from formatting discrepancies (e.g., abbreviated titles). The page links this spike to mid-2024 and to LLMs like ChatGPT; Nature reported many 2025 publications might include invalid references generated by AI. Fabricated citations are treated as a form of research integrity violation and are grounds for scrutiny and possible retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation / AI-manipulated imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of AI or other means to alter images in manuscripts (e.g., superimposing elements like a tape ruler) or duplicated/repeated image patterns in microscopy that indicate manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a New England Journal of Medicine clinical image retracted after authors acknowledged using AI to alter the photo, and a Journal of Materials Chemistry B paper retracted for repeating electron microscopy patterns and identical cell images across papers. Such manipulations can prompt retraction and media attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation stuffing / citation manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference proceedings or publications showing signs of citation stuffing or manipulation intended to favor particular authors (e.g., excess citations to a specific researcher).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites a blog post alleging citation stuffing in ACM conference proceedings tied to a particular chair; the resulting legal action (defamation suit) and court outcome illustrate that citation manipulation is a detectable misconduct pattern with reputational and legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism / pattern of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive or repeated plagiarism across works (books, papers, posters) such that a 'pattern of plagiarism' is identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal court ordered repayment of grant funding after a foundation found 'massive' misconduct and a pattern of plagiarism in two grant-funded books; in another case, overlaps between a students’ poster and a published article triggered misconduct allegations. Repeated/planned plagiarism can lead to funding repayment, publication retractions, and bans on applying for grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication of data (intentional falsification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate fabrication of data in grant-supported papers, unpublished manuscripts, presentations, and grant applications (e.g., described case of a scientist who intentionally fabricated data in multiple works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. Office of Research Integrity (ORI) announced a 15-year funding debarment for a scientist found to have fabricated data in numerous items. Administrative findings and Federal Register notices can formalize sanctions such as debarment from receiving federal funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science fair eligibility and timeline requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that student research projects must meet to be eligible for certain competitions (example: ViSEF requirement that a project had to have been completed in 12 months while student-authors continued their school work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of cheating or plagiarism at the science-fair level can arise when a project appears unusually advanced or overlaps substantially with existing published work; failing to meet explicit timeline or originality requirements can render a project ineligible and trigger investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication/identical images across publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that images or graphs in one work are identical or nearly identical to those in another publication (e.g., identical cell images, graphs reproduced with minor cosmetic changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such duplication (even if recolored or resized) is cited as an indicator of possible data misuse or access to others’ raw data and has led to misconduct allegations and retractions when detected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and detection of AI-generated survey responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that AI chatbots might complete online research surveys; detection tools can flag responses likely not written by humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preprint reported fewer than 1% of ~4,800 survey responses were likely non-human across 12 companies, but one company had ~16% flagged; the study used a detection tool created by Prolific. Monitoring for bot/AI responses is a recommended quality-control practice for survey-based research.
